You express "whatever happens" concession at B2 level: qualunque cosa succeda, chiunque venga, dovunque tu vada, comunque vada, per quanto sia difficile, costi quel che costi, che tu lo voglia o no.
the cover; the diner (in a restaurant)
Whatever happens, the trattoria opens at twelve.
However tired she is, she never complains.
Wherever you go, take this sentence with you.
To use qualunque / qualsiasi + noun + subjunctive.
To use chiunque, dovunque and comunque + subjunctive.
To use qualunque cosa (and the literary checché) + subjunctive.
To use per quanto + subjunctive, including with adjectives: per quanto stanca sia.
To use the fixed formulas: vada come vada, costi quel che costi, sia come sia, che tu lo voglia o no.
To encourage and make promises at a difficult moment.

Florence, May. Tomorrow morning Graziella has her operation. This evening she insisted on serving the last dinner before hospital. After closing, in the kitchen, she gives Karl her final instructions.
So, listen carefully. Whatever happens tomorrow, the trattoria opens at twelve.
Even if the operation lasts all day?
However the operation goes. People have to eat. And whoever comes in, you feed them. Even if they have no money.
Even the tourists who order cappuccino with pizza?
Even them. However much it makes me suffer. But cappuccino only until eleven.
And what if I get the ribollita wrong?
You won't. Whatever you put in the soffritto, except garlic, it'll come out good. I taught you.
A little. But come what may, I've had a good life. And a good trattoria. And some good restorers who can't cook.
Tomorrow evening I'll bring you ribollita in hospital. Whether the doctors like it or not.
Tomorrow evening I'll be asleep. But the day after, yes. And bring it hot.
"che lo vogliano o no" = whether they like it or not
Stress on the last syllable: chec-CHÉ. Double CC.
Qualunque decisione tu prenda, ti sosterremo.
Whatever decision you make, we'll support you.
A qualunque ora tu arrivi, la porta è aperta.
Whatever time you arrive, the door is open.
"Qualunque" and "qualsiasi" are invariable and always come BEFORE a singular noun: qualunque persona, qualsiasi giorno.
"Comunque" followed by a verb = "however it…" and takes the subjunctive. On its own, at the start of a sentence, it means "anyway, in any case" and takes nothing.
Qualunque cosa tu metta nel soffritto, verrà buona.
Qualsiasi cosa dicano i medici, io torno.
Checché ne dicano i critici, il film è riuscito.
"Checché ne dica" = whatever he says (about it). You'll come across it in articles and essays; in speech people say "qualunque cosa dica".
Per quanto io provi, non ci riesco.
Per quanto stanca sia, non si lamenta.
However tired she is, she doesn't complain.
Per quanto presto arriviate, troverete la fila.
However early you come, you'll find a queue.
Compare with chapter 69 (benché, sebbene): there the concession is about a real fact; here it's about an intensity or a possibility, "however much".
whatever it costs, at any price
che tu lo voglia o no
whether you like it or not
They are "frozen" subjunctives, learned as expressions. "Vada come vada" is the most used: you say it before an exam, an operation, a departure.
Come what may, I've had a good life.
Whether you like it or not, tomorrow we're going to the doctor.
Che cosa deve succedere domani, secondo Graziella?
La trattoria deve aprire alle dodici
A chi bisogna dare da mangiare?
A chiunque entri, anche senza soldi
Fino a che ora si serve il cappuccino?
Che cosa non si deve mettere nel soffritto?
Quando Karl porterà la ribollita in ospedale?

The evening before the operation, Graziella insisted on serving dinner as on every Tuesday. Nobody could persuade her to stay in bed. She put on her white apron, lit the stove, made ribollita, pappa al pomodoro and grandma's cake, and served forty-two covers with her usual determined step, greeting every customer by name. Only those who knew her well noticed that every now and then she stopped, leaning on the counter, with a hand on her chest. At half past ten, when the last customer had left, she locked the door, turned the sign to "Closed" and called Karl, Pietro and Matei into the kitchen. She was holding a handwritten sheet, in her big, crooked handwriting. "These are the instructions," she said. "Whatever happens tomorrow, the trattoria opens at twelve. Not at a quarter past twelve. At twelve."

The sheet had twelve points, numbered. The first said: "Whoever comes in, feed them. Even if they have no money. Especially if they have no money." The second: "Signor Franco wants his soup lukewarm, not hot. Don't ask him anything: just bring it." The third: "Cappuccino is served to tourists only until eleven, however much it makes me suffer." The fourth was about the fishmonger, the fifth the baker, the sixth the fruit seller, "who'll give you a discount even if she says she won't". The seventh said only: "No garlic." The last points were shorter. The tenth: "Lupino eats at seven, not before, however much he looks at you." The eleventh: "If anyone asks about me, say I'm on holiday." The twelfth was written smaller, at the bottom of the sheet, almost hidden: "However it goes, you've been good." Pietro read it twice. Then he folded the sheet and put it in his pocket, close to his heart.

That night, on the first floor, nobody really managed to sleep. Giulia and Matei sat in the kitchen until one, talking quietly about the next day's shifts, as if organising everything down to the last detail could protect Graziella from the hospital. Viola woke up twice and asked whether Granny Graziella was asleep. Pietro, in his room, reread the sheet of instructions ten times, by the light of the lamp, until he knew it by heart. Then he opened the black notebook and tried to write, but the words wouldn't come. In the end he wrote only the date and one sentence: "However hard I try not to think about it, I can't." At about two he heard light footsteps in the corridor and opened the door. It was Graziella, in her dressing gown, going to the kitchen to check the gas was off. They looked at each other in silence. "Go to sleep," she said. "You too, Grandma," he replied. Neither of them went straight away.

Afterwards, when Pietro and Matei had gone upstairs, Graziella stayed alone in the kitchen with Karl. She gave him the last instructions about the ribollita, then sat down on the stool and for a long moment said nothing, looking at the cold stove. Karl asked her, quietly, whether she was afraid. Graziella thought about it. "A little," she said. "But come what may, I've had a good life. And a good trattoria. And some good restorers who can't cook." Karl laughed, though his eyes were moist. He promised that the next day he would bring her ribollita in hospital, whether the doctors liked it or not. "Tomorrow evening I'll be asleep," replied Graziella. "But the day after, yes. And bring it hot." Then she got up, patted him on the shoulder, as you do with a colleague, and climbed the stairs slowly, holding the handrail. Karl stayed in the kitchen another hour, in the dark, sitting on her stool. He couldn't bring himself to leave.

The next morning, at half past six, Marco drove his mother to Careggi hospital, in silence. Pietro sat in the back, with Graziella's bag on his knees: inside were a new nightdress, the slippers Guido had made, Aldo's photograph, Viola's drawing of the heart with the plaster, and a glass jar without a label that Graziella had put in at the last moment and that nobody was to open. On the ward they were met by a young nurse, who recognised Marco and shook his hand. Graziella was told to lie down on a bed; they put a plastic bracelet with her name on her and a blue gown that she looked at with disgust. "I look like a painting before restoration," she said. Then the surgeon arrived, Dr Bianchi, a tall, calm man, who explained once more how the operation would go. Graziella listened to the end. Then she asked him a single question: "Do you eat ribollita?"

The surgeon was taken aback for a moment. Then he smiled and said that yes, he did, but that his had always been made by his grandmother, in Prato, and that since she died he had never found a good one. Graziella nodded, satisfied, as if he had passed an exam. "Then you know what it means to do things with care," she said. "Please. The heart is like a soffritto. It has to be done slowly." Dr Bianchi promised. Then the nurse said it was time. Before they took her away, Graziella called Pietro to the bed and took his hand. She said nothing solemn. She told him to remember to feed Lupino at seven, to check that Karl didn't put garlic in, and to call the neighbour on the second floor, who was worried. Then, as the bed was already leaving the room, she turned and added: "Wherever I go now, I'm coming back. Do you understand? I'm coming back."

When the bed disappeared behind the doors of the operating theatre, Pietro stood in the middle of the corridor, his grandmother's bag in his hand, not knowing what to do. It was his father who took him by the shoulders and led him away, towards the waiting room. They walked in silence. Then Marco, without looking at him, said something he had never said. "Did you know I was afraid of her when I was little?" Pietro looked at him in amazement. "She was very strict," Marco went on. "She never let me go out before I'd finished my homework, she made me peel potatoes on Saturdays, she told me off if I was rude to customers. I thought she didn't love me. Then, at sixteen, I had an accident on my moped. Nothing serious. But when I woke up in hospital, she was there, sitting by the bed, still in her apron. She had closed the trattoria. For me." He stopped. "That's when I understood."

The operation would last five hours, perhaps six. The waiting room of the cardiac surgery ward was a long white room, with orange plastic chairs lined up along the wall, a coffee machine that made a strange noise, and a window overlooking a car park. At eight there were Marco, Sara and Pietro. At nine Bellini arrived, with his stick and his newspaper, which he never read. At ten Giulia and Viola arrived; Viola had brought another drawing and a box of felt-tips to make more. At eleven Efisio arrived, who said nothing and sat in a corner with his hat on his knees. At noon Rita arrived, Davide's mother, who worked at Careggi itself, on the next ward, and had changed her shift specially. She brought six real coffees, from the hospital bar, "because the machine coffee is bad for the heart, and today one sick heart is enough".

At two in the afternoon Davide arrived too, straight from school, with his rucksack and sketchbook. He sat down next to Viola and for an hour they drew together, in silence, she with felt-tips and he with a pencil. Davide drew the waiting room just as it was: the orange chairs, the coffee machine, the window over the car park, and the people one by one, Marco pacing, Bellini with his closed newspaper, Efisio with his hat. In the centre, above the theatre door, he drew a stopped clock. Meanwhile Pietro's phone kept vibrating. It was Karl, every half hour, with the same question. It was Ruggeri, from Rome, writing: "Whatever happens, we're with you." It was Dr Ferraris, from Milan: "However it goes, today's ribollita is on me." It was don Paolo, who wrote only: "I've lit a candle. Just one. For the varnish." Pietro laughed for the first time all day.

Meanwhile, in via Maggio, at twelve on the dot, Karl opened the trattoria door. He had slept three hours. At four he was already in the kitchen, and by six the ribollita was resting in the big pot, ready to be boiled again. Matei was at the stove with him, in an apron that was too short. Chiara was at the till, with a calculator and a notebook, swearing she wouldn't touch anything that could burn. Davide and Valeria waited at tables. On the door, under Davide's sign, "Graziella is resting. The trattoria isn't", someone had added during the night, in marker, another line: "Come on, Graziella." Nobody ever found out who it was. At five past twelve the first customer came in: Signor Franco, ninety, with his stick and his hat, who had come even though it was Tuesday and not Thursday. He sat down at his table and asked for nothing. Karl, remembering point two, brought him his soup lukewarm.

At a quarter to one came the first crisis. Karl, distracted by a message from Pietro that said only "nothing yet", left the soffritto on the heat too long. When he noticed, the onion was already dark and the smell of burning was reaching the dining room. For a second Karl stood paralysed, ladle in hand, like a student who has got everything wrong in an exam. It was Matei who moved first. He turned off the heat, threw out the soffritto, took a clean pan and put it in his hand. "Start again," he said. "Slowly. Low heat. As she says." Karl breathed. He started again. However much of a hurry he was in, he cut the onion slowly, put it in the pan with cold oil and watched it turn transparent, without taking his eyes off it. Ten minutes later the soffritto was perfect. Matei patted him on the shoulder. "You see?" he said. "In restoration too, when you get it wrong, you remove everything and start again. It's not a tragedy. It's the job."

By half past twelve the trattoria was full. They weren't the usual customers: they were everyone. There was the fruit seller, who never ate out and had closed her stall at the market for an hour that day. There was Guido, still in his leather apron. There were the baker and his wife, the barmaid, the two brothers from the newsstand, the lawyer Bardi, who ordered the ribollita and said he was eating it "out of institutional solidarity". There was don Paolo, who had come from San Leonardo on the first train. There was even Dr Ferraris, who was in Florence on business and had heard everything from Karl. Nobody talked about Graziella. But whenever someone came in, the first thing they did was look at Karl, and Karl, every time, shook his head: nothing yet. At two the ribollita was running out. Matei made another pot, even though he knew it wouldn't have time to rest.

At about two a boy nobody knew came in, a twenty-year-old foreigner with an enormous rucksack on his back and worn-out shoes, who stopped in the doorway and looked at the full room with an embarrassed air. He asked in English, quietly, whether there was anything that cost less than five euros. Chiara, at the till, looked at Karl. Karl remembered the first point of the instructions, the one Pietro had read him the evening before: "Whoever comes in, feed them. Especially if they have no money." He sat the boy at the table by the kitchen and brought him a bowl of ribollita, bread, a glass of water. The boy ate in silence, very slowly, like someone who hasn't had a hot meal for days. When he asked for the bill, Karl told him it was already paid. The boy didn't understand. Before leaving he left a note on the table, written in English on a paper napkin: "Thank you. Whoever Graziella is, I hope she gets well."

In hospital, time didn't pass. By two Viola had used up the box of felt-tips and had drawn all the people in the waiting room, one per sheet, with their names written underneath in capitals. Bellini, who hadn't opened his newspaper, told Pietro quietly about the day of his stent, Graziella's thermos, the ribollita eaten with a plastic spoon. Efisio, in his corner, had taken out of his pocket a wooden rosary, which nobody knew he had, and was passing it through his fingers without moving his lips. Marco paced up and down the corridor, and every time a door opened he stopped dead. Sara told him to sit down. He sat down, and after a minute got up again. At half past two a nurse came out of the operating theatre and they all stood up together. But the nurse walked past without looking at them. She was going to fetch something. They sat down again, one at a time.

At a quarter past three the door opened again, and this time Dr Bianchi came out, still wearing his green cap. He stopped in front of Marco. In the waiting room nobody breathed. The surgeon took off his mask and said only: "It went well." Then he explained that the operation had been long but without complications, that the new bypass was working, that the heart had started beating well on its own again. Graziella was in intensive care, asleep, and would stay there at least until the next day. They could see her only through the window, one at a time, for a few minutes. Marco covered his face with his hands. Sara hugged him. Efisio made the sign of the cross and put the rosary back in his pocket. Bellini leaned on his stick and closed his eyes. And Viola, who hadn't understood everything but had understood the essential, ran to Dr Bianchi and gave him one of her drawings: him, in his white coat, with a brush in his hand.

Pietro sent Karl a message, a single word: "Good." In the trattoria, Karl read his phone, put it down on the counter and stood motionless for a second. Then he raised his head and said it aloud, to the whole room: "It went well." There was a moment's silence, then the trattoria exploded. The fruit seller started crying. Guido banged his fist on the table so hard the glasses jumped. The lawyer Bardi stood up and applauded, and after him everyone else. Don Paolo said a short prayer, aloud, which nobody expected and everyone listened to standing up. Dr Ferraris ordered a bottle of wine for every table and paid for it himself, "whatever it costs". Signor Franco, the only one still seated, finished his lukewarm soup, wiped his mouth with his napkin and said to Karl: "Tell her the soup was good. But not like hers." Karl promised he would tell her. Word for word.

That evening, after closing, the cooperative kids all sat round the big table, as tired as after a night of flooding. Chiara counted the takings twice and announced the number: a hundred and eighteen covers. Matei said he had never worked so hard in his life, not even during the Malta restoration. Karl said nothing: his hands were still red from the hot water and his eyes were closing on their own. Davide pinned the foreign boy's note on the kitchen shelf, next to Viola's drawing. At about eleven Bellini arrived, accompanied by Efisio, straight from the hospital. He sat at his table, looked at the empty room, the washed plates, the clean big pot, and said only: "Good people." Then he asked whether there was any ribollita left. There was, a single bowl, at the bottom of the pot. Karl brought it to him. Bellini ate it slowly, in silence. "Ninety-eight," he said at the end, smiling. "But don't tell her. She wants to be the one giving the marks."

That evening Pietro was able to see his grandmother through the intensive care window, for five minutes. She was lying in a bed full of tubes and wires, with a mask on her face and her eyes closed, and she seemed much smaller than she had ever been. The screens next to the bed showed green numbers and a line going up and down, regular as the breathing of someone asleep. Pietro stood looking at her with his hands on the glass. He thought of all the times he had seen her on her feet, ladle in hand, shouting orders in the kitchen. He thought of the 1966 photograph, the twelve-year-old girl with the tray of sandwiches in the mud. He thought that, however well he had known her all his life, he had never seen her like this. Still. Then the nurse touched his shoulder. It was time. Before leaving, Pietro wrote with his finger on the misted glass a word nobody saw: "Come back."

Walking home that night, along the avenue that ran down from the Careggi hill towards the city, Marco told Pietro where rule number one came from, the one his mother always repeated. His grandfather Renzo, Graziella's father, had told him when he was a child. In 1950, the year they opened the trattoria, Renzo and his wife Lucia had almost nothing: six tables, a borrowed kitchen, debts with the baker. One winter evening a thin man came in, in a coat full of holes, who asked if he could sit in the warm. He had no money. Renzo gave him a bowl of soup. The man came back every evening for a month, and Renzo fed him every evening. Then the man disappeared. Six months later a letter arrived from Milan, with some money inside and a note: he had found work, and the money was to pay for the soups. "From that day," said Marco, "that's been the rule in the trattoria. Whoever comes in."

Graziella woke up the next morning, at a quarter past seven. The nurse on duty later told Marco that she had opened her eyes slowly, looked at the ceiling, then the machines, then her, and asked her first question in a hoarse voice, barely audible. The nurse had bent down to understand, convinced she was asking for water, or wanted to know where she was, or how the operation had gone. Instead Graziella had asked: "How many covers?" The nurse hadn't understood. Graziella had repeated, louder: "Yesterday. At the trattoria. How many covers?" Marco, when they told him, laughed so loudly he had to go out into the corridor. Then he phoned Chiara, who had the till notebook. "A hundred and eighteen," said Chiara. "Double a normal Tuesday." Marco went back into the room and told his mother. Graziella closed her eyes, satisfied. "Good," she murmured. "And the garlic?" "No garlic, Mum." "Good," she repeated. And fell asleep again.

The day after that, as he had promised, Karl went to the hospital with a thermos of hot ribollita, wrapped in a towel so it wouldn't cool. The nurses told him it wasn't allowed, that on the ward patients ate only what the hospital kitchen sent up. Karl explained, in his most formal Italian, that it was a specific therapy, prescribed by the patient herself, and that he took full responsibility. The nurses looked at each other. Then one of them, the oldest, opened the thermos, sniffed, and said only: "One spoonful. Just one. And I didn't see anything." Graziella, sitting up in bed with pillows behind her back, ate the spoonful with her eyes closed. Then she ate another, while the nurse pretended to look out of the window. Then she looked at Karl. "Ninety-nine," she said. "You didn't put enough pepper. But ninety-nine." Karl had to go out into the corridor too.

Graziella stayed in hospital nine days. They were nine days during which, as Dr Bianchi put it, the cardiac surgery ward at Careggi was in practice run by a seventy-five-year-old patient with a mobile phone. Graziella phoned the trattoria three times a day: at ten, to find out what was on the menu; at three, to find out how many covers; at eleven at night, to find out whether they had turned the gas off properly. She gave the nurses advice on the patients' diet. She persuaded an old gentleman in the next room, who wouldn't eat, to finish his broth "because broth isn't to be wasted". Rita, who worked nights on the neighbouring ward, dropped in to see her at two, when she wasn't sleeping, and the two women talked quietly about children, night shifts, how hard it is to be the one who takes care of others. "However tired you are," Graziella told her one night, "never tell anyone. Except me."

On the fifth day Bellini came too, with his stick, a bunch of flowers and a travel chess set, because Dr Bianchi had said the patient had to stay calm and not think about the trattoria. Graziella looked at the chess set suspiciously. "I can't play," she said. "I'll teach you," replied Bellini. They played all afternoon. Graziella lost the first three games and won the fourth, then accused Bellini of letting her win, and Bellini swore he hadn't, and neither believed the other. At the end, while the nurse took away the dinner tray, Graziella asked him quietly whether he had been afraid, on the day of the operation. Bellini thought about it. "Yes," he said. "More than when I had mine." Graziella nodded. "I was more afraid than you, that day, too," she said. "We're two stubborn old people." "Two old mules," Bellini corrected. And for the first time in many years they laughed together like two kids.

On the last day, before being discharged, Graziella called Pietro to the bed and asked him to get her bag. Inside, under the nightdress and Guido's slippers, was still the glass jar without a label. Graziella took it out, looked at it for a long time, then put it back in the bag. "Not yet," she said, more to herself than to Pietro. Then she asked him about the black notebook, and whether he had written anything in those days. Pietro said yes, but that he didn't want to read it to her. Graziella smiled. "Then I'll tell you something, and you write it down," she said. "Whatever you do in life, restorer, journalist, teacher, whatever you like, remember that important things are done like a soffritto. Slowly. On a low heat. And without walking away while they cook." Pietro wrote it down that very evening, in the black notebook, word for word, under point number twelve of the instruction sheet, which he had stuck onto the page.

On the tenth day Graziella came back to via Maggio, in Marco's car, with her bag on her knees and Guido's slippers on her feet. When the car turned into the street, she saw a small crowd in front of the trattoria. Everyone was there: the fruit seller, Guido, the baker, Efisio, Valeria, Bellini with his stick, the cooperative kids, Viola with a bunch of violets in her hand, and old Signor Franco, sitting on a chair someone had brought out for him. Above the door, Davide had hung a new sign, hand-painted: "Graziella is back. So is the trattoria." Graziella got out of the car slowly, leaning on Marco's arm. She looked at the sign, then at the crowd, then at the open door of her trattoria, from which came the smell of ribollita. Nobody said anything. Then Graziella straightened up, adjusted her coat and said, in her usual voice: "Well? What are you all doing out here? There's work to do inside."
Che cosa diceva il primo punto delle istruzioni?
Che domanda ha fatto Graziella al chirurgo?
Se poteva tornare a casa subito
Che cosa ha chiesto Graziella appena sveglia?
Quanti coperti c’erano stati in trattoria
Che voto dà Graziella alla ribollita portata da Karl?
Che cosa dice Graziella tornando in via Maggio?
Wherever you go, think of us.
However tired I am, I'll finish.
A few points from the sheet Graziella left. Read and answer.
One: whoever comes in, feed them. Even if they have no money. Especially if they have no money.
Three: cappuccino is served to tourists only until eleven, however much it makes me suffer.
Ten: Lupino eats at seven, not before, however much he looks at you.
Twelve: however it goes, you've been good.

Write (22–24 sentences) a list of instructions and good wishes for someone taking your place for a while (at home, at work, with a pet) or a letter of encouragement before a difficult moment. Use all the structures in the chapter.
I used qualunque / qualsiasi + noun + subjunctive.
I used chiunque, dovunque and comunque + subjunctive.
I used qualunque cosa or checché + subjunctive.
I used per quanto + subjunctive (also with an adjective).
I used at least two fixed formulas (vada come vada, costi quel che costi, che tu lo voglia o no).
Dear Ana, here are the instructions for the two weeks you'll be staying at my place.
Whatever happens, the cat eats at eight. However much she miaows, don't give her anything before.
Whoever rings the doorbell, don't open if you don't know them.
And however Thursday's exam goes, I'm proud of you. Come what may, there's a cake waiting for you.
Say ten promises or wishes with qualunque cosa, chiunque, dovunque, comunque and per quanto.
Encourage a friend aloud before an exam, using three fixed formulas.
Retell in 5 minutes the day of the operation, from Graziella's instructions to her return to via Maggio.
